documents.unit: AI at Carleton (Academic AI Advisory Team)
documents.title: Policies - AI at Carleton
documents.stance_why: The page does not ban or encourage AI; it requires that "the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves" and otherwise leaves detail to faculty. Because AI help is implicitly allowed so long as that condition holds, I code it permit (with conditions) rather than delegates, since the college sets the student rule itself.
documents.summary: College-wide AI policy page. It gives employees data-security rules for generative AI (Gemini allowed with Carleton accounts for low and medium risk data) and says the reworded Academic Integrity policy expects students to do the core intellectual substance of assignments themselves, with faculty encouraged to discuss AI with students.

units.why: The page opens by saying "existing policies still apply to AI" while new ones may be needed; this is the institution-level framing of scope and principles for AI, so P56 (framework/preamble) fits better than P54, which concerns review cycles.
units.anchor: In many cases, Carleton’s existing policies still apply to AI
units.frag_start: AI technologies raise novel questions around

units.why: "highlight any additions and changes as they’re made" commits the page to tracking policy changes over time, so it is a revisit/update commitment (P54).
units.anchor: highlight any additions and changes as they’re made
units.frag_start: This page will provide links to
units.policy: The AI policies page highlights additions and changes to AI policies as they are made.

units.why: "should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools" is a prohibition-style directive on employees about data; it is data protection (P50), and it binds employees rather than students.
units.anchor: Carleton employees should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools
units.frag_start: Carleton employees should not enter
units.policy: Carleton employees should not enter sensitive data or proprietary content into generative AI tools.

units.why: Naming Google Gemini as the one exception, usable with Carleton accounts for low and medium risk data, points to a vetted tool: P50 (prefer vetted tools) rather than P17 because it is a data-handling permission, not a course tool.
units.anchor: welcome to submit low and medium risk data
units.frag_start: Given these stipulations, Carleton community members
units.policy: Carleton community members are welcome to submit low and medium risk data into Google Gemini when logged in through their Carleton accounts.

units.why: "Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data" is an absolute data-protection rule, so P50 with must-not force; the text uses "should" but "under no circumstances" makes it a prohibition.
units.anchor: Under no circumstances should individuals share
units.frag_start: Under no circumstances should individuals share
units.policy: Under no circumstances should individuals share high risk data (e.g. SSN or credit card information) with Gemini.

units.why: "please contact infosec" before sharing medium risk data with other vendors including other generative AI tools is a request to consult security first; it is a data-protection step (P50).
units.anchor: Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors
units.frag_start: Before sharing medium risk data with
units.policy: Before sharing medium risk data with outside vendors, including other generative AI tools, people contact infosec@carleton.edu.

units.why: The sentence says the Academic Integrity policy was reworded to articulate AI use in students' academic work, i.e. AI misuse is dealt with under the integrity policy (P36); it is a fact, so modality informs.
units.anchor: Carleton recently reworded its Academic Integrity policy
units.frag_start: Carleton recently reworded its Academic
units.policy: Carleton reworded its Academic Integrity policy to articulate guidelines around AI use in students' academic work.

units.why: Students must complete assignments so "the core intellectual substance" is carried out by themselves; this requires submitted work to be their own (P29) and is the operative AI rule, not a ban or a permission.
units.anchor: core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves
units.frag_start: the crucial phrase is that students
units.policy: Students are expected to complete all assignments in a manner ensuring that the core intellectual substance of the assignment is carried out by the student themselves.

units.why: "the responsibility lies with each student to ensure that they identify and complete the core intellectual substance" places responsibility on the student, so P29.
units.anchor: the responsibility lies with each student
units.frag_start: Ultimately, the responsibility lies with each
units.policy: The responsibility lies with each student to ensure that they identify and complete the core intellectual substance of their work.

units.why: Faculty are "encouraged to discuss this with students" including how AI tools "might assist or hinder" learning; no type covers instructor-student discussion of AI, and P41 is about limiting AI, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to discuss this with students
units.frag_start: But faculty are encouraged to discuss
units.policy: Faculty are encouraged to discuss with students, generally and about AI specifically, what the work of their courses is meant to be, how it benefits learning, and how AI tools might assist or hinder that learning.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors are encouraged to discuss the purpose of coursework and AI's help or harm to learning with students.

documents.unit: Writing Across the Curriculum (Working with AI, resources for faculty)
documents.title: AI Course Policies
documents.stance_why: The page is advice for instructors on writing their own AI policies and says "those decisions are ultimately up to you"; it offers templates that "ban almost all AI use, allow some AI use, and allow all AI use". It sets no stance itself, so delegates, with the three templates as tiers.
documents.summary: Writing Across the Curriculum guidance telling faculty how to craft course AI policies: learn what the tools do, decide which uses to permit or forbid, state the policy on the syllabus and each assignment, explain the rationale, and keep an open dialogue with students. It treats detection as unreliable and relies on trust.

units.why: Advising instructors to build a working knowledge of what AI tools can do is support for faculty learning about AI before setting policy (P63).
units.anchor: Start with a working knowledge of what current AI tools can do.
units.frag_start: Start with a working knowledge

units.why: "Seriously consider what writing tasks you want students to do themselves" asks each instructor to decide per course what AI use to allow; per-instructor choice is P04.
units.anchor: Seriously consider what writing tasks you want students to do themselves
units.frag_start: Seriously consider what writing tasks
units.frag_end: could reasonably do with AI tools.

units.why: Instructors should "explain the rationale" for why certain AI uses undermine the course's value, i.e. explaining that AI use can undercut learning; P41 is nearest, and P09 is not chosen because this is about explanation rather than the syllabus statement.
units.anchor: explain the rationale behind them. Why would certain uses of AI undermine the value
units.frag_start: Set clear guidelines for your students
units.policy: Instructors set clear AI guidelines for students and explain the rationale behind them, including why certain uses of AI would undermine the value of the course or assignments for them.

units.why: "State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus" asks instructors for a syllabus AI statement (P09).
units.anchor: State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus
units.frag_start: State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus
units.policy: State your AI policies clearly on the syllabus.

units.why: Reiterating the policy on each major assignment prompt, especially if prohibitions vary over the term, is about AI expectations in assignment instructions (P09).
units.anchor: reiterate them on the prompts for each major assignment
units.frag_start: and reiterate them on the prompts
units.frag_end: vary over the course of the term.
units.policy: Instructors reiterate their AI policies on the prompts for each major assignment, especially if assignments require different intellectual work or prohibitions vary over the term.

units.why: Encouraging students to come to the instructor with questions about AI tools is the ask-first norm (P10), here framed from the instructor's side.
units.anchor: encourage them to come to you with questions about AI tools
units.frag_start: Expressing trust in their desire to learn
units.frag_end: how to use them in your course.
units.policy: Instructors maintain an open dialogue and encourage students to come to them with questions about AI tools and how to use them in the course.

units.why: The page says telling students "don't use AI in your writing, period" is not practical or desirable because nearly everyone uses spell check and similar tools; this is a view on the default rule, and P04 fits best because the guide then leaves the decision to instructors.
units.anchor: it may be tempting to simply tell students “don’t use AI in your writing, period,”
units.frag_start: So while it may be tempting to simply
units.policy: A blanket ban on AI in student writing is not a practical or particularly desirable solution.

units.why: Noting that some AI applications let students focus on important aspects by easing ancillary tasks (grammar, citations, proofreading) is a permitted-use statement about AI in prose, so P18.
units.anchor: some applications of AI can actually help them focus on the most important aspects
units.frag_start: Depending on the kinds of intellectual work
units.policy: Some applications of AI can help students focus on the most important aspects of assignments by making ancillary tasks such as grammar, citations and proofreading easier to manage.

units.why: The page says instructors may decide that students should work on grammar and similar skills themselves, since those tasks may be a fundamental part of the work; the decision is the instructor's (P04).
units.anchor: those decisions are ultimately up to you
units.frag_start: Of course, you may also decide that you
units.frag_end: those decisions are ultimately up to you.
units.policy: Whether students work on tasks such as grammar, citations and proofreading without AI is up to the instructor.

units.why: The list of reported student uses is followed by the statement that it is reasonable to allow, "or even to explicitly require", some of them; the decision is the instructor's, so P04, unit stance permit.
units.anchor: reasonable to allow, or even to explicitly
units.frag_start: but it’s also fairly easy to imagine assignments
units.policy: In some courses and assignments it is reasonable to allow, or even to explicitly require, students to use some AI techniques; the decision is the instructor's, based on the learning wanted.

units.why: A complete syllabus policy should answer five questions, beginning with how students are permitted to use AI and what is forbidden; this is a content list for the syllabus statement (P09).
units.anchor: a complete policy would address
units.frag_start: In the case of AI specifically, a complete policy would address
units.frag_end: What uses of AI are explicitly forbidden in your class?
units.policy: A complete AI policy addresses how students are permitted to use AI and what uses are explicitly forbidden.

units.why: The list asks how students should "document, cite, or otherwise disclose" AI use if allowed, so instructors should specify disclosure (P24).
units.anchor: how do you want students to document, cite, or otherwise disclose
units.frag_start: If any use of AI is allowed, how do you want students
units.policy: If any use of AI is allowed, the policy states how students document, cite, or otherwise disclose the ways they use AI to complete assignments.

units.why: The guide says a policy should state whether rules vary by assignment and that assignments that deviate need their own clear AI policy; this concerns assignment-level AI statements (P09), not P04 since it asks for writing the variation down.
units.anchor: you’ll also need to write clear AI policies for any assignment that deviates
units.frag_start: Will the rules around AI vary from one assignment
units.policy: Where AI rules vary from one assignment to the next, a clear AI policy is written for any assignment that deviates from the general course policy.

units.why: Stating the overall rationale of the policy and how it fits the course goals is the explanatory-rationale advice, P41 as above.
units.anchor: What is the overall rationale behind this policy?
units.frag_start: What is the overall rationale behind this policy?
units.frag_end: intellectual work you want your students to do?
units.policy: The AI policy states its overall rationale and how it fits the course goals and the intellectual work students are to do.

units.why: "explanatory rather than punitive" is advice on the tone of syllabus statements; no type covers writing style of the statement, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: explanatory rather than punitive
units.frag_start: As a general rule, the best syllabus statements
units.policy: Syllabus AI statements are clear, concise, and explanatory rather than punitive.
units.uncovered_note: Advice on the style and tone of syllabus statements (clear, explanatory, not punitive).

units.why: Saying a syllabus may be general and need not cover every tool or contingency is about the scope of the syllabus statement (P09), a permission to be general.
units.anchor: you don’t need to address every possible tool, use, or contingency
units.frag_start: Thus, you don’t need to address every possible tool
units.frag_end: over the course of a term.
units.policy: A syllabus AI statement can be general and need not address every possible tool, use, or contingency.

units.why: Putting a more specific AI policy in the prompt of every major writing assignment is a best practice for assignment-level expectations (P09); a simple pointer to the syllabus suffices if rules do not vary.
units.anchor: include a more specific version of your AI policy as part of the prompt
units.frag_start: That said, it’s probably best practice
units.frag_end: for every major writing assignment in your course.
units.policy: It is best practice to include a more specific version of the AI policy in the prompt for every major writing assignment.

units.why: Instructors should discuss the policy in class, at the latest before the first major writing assignment, and let students ask questions; there is no type for classroom discussion of the policy, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: be prepared to spend some time discussing them in class
units.frag_start: Finally, regardless of the policies you set
units.policy: Instructors discuss their AI policies in class, addressing them by the time students begin the first major writing assignment, explaining the logic and giving students a chance to respond and ask questions.
units.uncovered_note: Instructors discuss the AI policy and its logic with students in class.

units.why: The page admits AI use is hard to detect and "virtually impossible to prove this conclusively", which is a point about detection being unreliable (P39).
units.anchor: it’s virtually impossible to prove this conclusively
units.frag_start: Even if you do “detect” AI writing
units.policy: Detecting AI writing is difficult, and it is virtually impossible to prove conclusively that a product was produced with undue help from AI.

units.why: The page says prohibitions "may also be unenforceable in practice" and instructors must "trust our students to follow our policies voluntarily"; this relies on student responsibility rather than policing (P60).
units.anchor: we will increasingly need to trust our students to follow our policies
units.frag_start: it does mean that we will increasingly need to
units.policy: Instructors will increasingly need to trust students to follow AI policies voluntarily, since prohibitions may be unenforceable in practice.

units.why: Instructors should explain what role the writing assignments serve and what skills students practice, as the reason for limiting AI; this is P41 (practice builds skill).
units.anchor: What role do the writing assignments serve in your course?
units.frag_start: What role do the writing assignments serve
units.policy: Instructors explain the role of writing assignments in the course and what knowledge students gain and what skills they practice.

units.why: Telling students that using AI to generate text or perfect grammar could diminish learning is an instruction to explain how AI use undermines the benefit of the assignment, P41.
units.anchor: How would using AI to generate text or perfect their grammar diminish students’ learning
units.frag_start: What uses of AI tools will (and possibly won’t) work
units.policy: Instructors explain how using AI to generate text or perfect grammar would diminish students' learning or undermine the benefits of completing the assignments without these tools.

units.why: Instructors should tell students about AI limitations, including unreliable quality and information, so students can weigh them; that matches P31 (AI output is often wrong).
units.anchor: What limitations of AI tools should they be aware of
units.frag_start: What limitations of AI tools should they be aware of
units.policy: Instructors explain the limitations of AI tools, including the quality of the writing they produce and the reliability of the information they synthesize.

units.why: Instructors should tell students what to do if unsure about a use of AI and when and how to ask, which is directly the ask-first rule (P10).
units.anchor: What should students do if they’re unsure about a particular use of AI
units.frag_start: What should students do if they’re unsure
units.frag_end: When and how should they ask you about it?
units.policy: Instructors explain what students should do if they are unsure about a particular use of AI, and when and how to ask.

units.why: Encouraging students to ask questions about AI applications not explicitly covered by the policy is the student-side ask-first norm (P10).
units.anchor: encourage them to ask questions, especially about applications of AI tools
units.frag_start: For the students’ part, encourage them to ask questions
units.policy: Students are encouraged to ask questions, especially about applications of AI tools that are not explicitly covered by the policies.

units.why: The resources list offers templates for policies that ban almost all, allow some, or allow all AI use; this names three tiers of course policy (P05).
units.anchor: Templates for policies that ban almost all AI use
units.frag_start: Templates for policies that ban
units.policy: Templates are available for policies that ban almost all AI use, allow some AI use, and allow all AI use.

notes: University layer only (no school or computing document collected). Doc 1 actor for data-security rules is 'all' because it binds employees generally. Three units are UNCOVERED: instructor-student discussion of AI (twice) and tone of syllabus statements.
